The concept of the game is quite unique and interesting - however very expandable. 

Storywise, being an operator within a surveillance program is portrayed as one would imagine it to be - without either condemning or idealizing such measures. To me that was a positive surprise. 

The game however is quite short. It took me roughly five hours without rushing and taking a lot of time reviewing all the material to actually finish it. I do understand that creating content to fit into that game takes time and effort. A second part has already been announced and I will surely buy that, too.

A really well executed visual novel style of game even though it doesn't look like one at all. 

It has some parallels to Uplink, the old hacker game, which is really nice, the stuff you "do" in the game is pretty cool, even if you technically don't "do" anything, you just press the buttons that the game tells you to press. 
Which brings me to the point of it having some really weirdly executed "multiple choice" paths, where if you accidentally select (or purposefully just to see what happens) some "wrong" option, the story can get really weird. It's basically a whodunit and your paranoid coworker/boss usually eggs you on to convict literally everyone, but if you try and pick some obviously false choice (I picked it because it seemed like proof that this person is a liar) he all of the sudden goes "ah it's okay, we got solid proof that this person is innocent" even though it's obvious as hell that the person is lying and five seconds later you find solid evidence of this person being guilty, he just goes "oh that's weird, they just said that they're innocent, oh well just a coincidence then, LOL!". 

It doesn't really detract from the game, it has an amazing feel to it and it really creeped me out at some points, because I've always thought if my identity can be traced from my online profiles and sometimes purposefully provide false info just to screw with my imaginary pursuers. This game made me feel that feeling of paranoia again, in a good, analytical way though. 

It's a shame though that the devs didn't make an Uplink-esque sort of game where you have randomized missions and you try and pick up info about random people, but like a couple of those random people are actually your targets, and it would be really nice if we came to that conclusion ourselves, not with a prompt "CLICK HERE" every few seconds. But one can only dream. It's still a good interactive story kinda game though. 

I think the price is a bit too steep for a VERY straightforward game where you literally just follow the prompt and there's very few in the way of different choices or stuff that you do by yourself, you can only come up with the solution, but surprise, it's the only possible solution. Sometimes it's a "find what I need to click to progress" sorta game, but still, the story is kinda neat and fun, definitely worth a grab when it's on sale.

Is this game a masterpiece? The game itself probably not, but the topics that the game raises are certainly worth of discussion:

Does spying on everyone help make our countries a safer place? Or does it just make everyone a potential terrorist and serve the ones that control the surveillance?

Does achieving your personal goals in which you really believe justify killing innocents???

Those are the main questions that you will have to answer for yourself if you play this little (kind of) interactive movie.

[Spoilers included]

I received the game as a gift and played it almost immediately. Interface was nice a little bit confusing at first, but Symes helped me out for the first part. Story turns very dark very quickly. Over time, a feeling of dread overwhelms me as I submit a vital-looking datachunk to be processed by Orwell. What feels real is how the use of hyperbolic sentences and phrases in the media, usually for comedic effect, can inadvertently be twisted into something that can target you as a threat to the government (case in point, Juliet talking about how Cassi 'tortures' her with muffins/cupcakes, and Symes believing 100% that Cassi indeed tortures Juliet). Scary to think how it would be in the real world.

This game has me reeling. As a fan of Orwell, especially 1984, this feels like a dream. I'm sad it wasn't longer, or that it just follows one track. It reminds me of Papers, Please, with the screening and processing and comparing of vital information. So I was kind of expecting literally screening suspicious targets in the whole country. Then again, the Thought arc was very well-thought out. Again, however, I didn't expect it to end so abruptly on the 5th day. Was hoping for more.

That twist during the conference call was great, but too convenient. The least suspected was the mastermind after all. But why? Were they romantically involved? Were there any signs of fanaticism, obsessive behavior? Don't get me wrong, I love how this played into the story. Just wondering if it's all to convenient for the plot so as to completely throw the investigator off.

Few technical issues, such as the dialogue boxes of the advisors (Delacroix/Symes) sometimes slow down the entire game. During chapter 5, while processing the last 4 datachunks before the call, Delacroix says a reminder and my game just bugs to oblivion. I can't see her message bubble, I can't click on anything. Not to change tabs, heck not even to bring down the main menu of the game. Had to quit the game and open again, thankfully it doesn't restart at the beginning of every day if you quit midway through a chapter, else I'd have never finished it. 

7.2 hours played, 2 endings down. Highly recommend and would get Orwell: Ignorance is Strength.

If you've watched the trailer and read the game description, you'll quickly understand your role in Orwell. You are an investigator, watching over the lives of a handful of citizens known for being anti-government. Your job is to find incriminating evidence on these individuals by reading through their text messages, emails, and pretty much anything digital that you can get your hands on. This premise alone was enough to interest me, and I was more than impressed by the results.

What you might not understand from the trailer is your ability to sympathize with the people you're supposed to be incriminating. There are consequences for every action and inaction. Orwell gave me power and I was immersed. What I wasn't expecting were the many surprises that were in store for me. I won't spoil any of them, but will say they were all worth spending the extra time exploring to discover.

My only faults with the game were points were it felt like I had hit a dead end. Throughout the game, there are icons indicating information you have not discovered to help guide you. However, there are also many pieces of hidden information which have no indicators that lead to achievements and, in some instances, progress the main storyline. With no indicators telling me there was more to be found, I had to watch playthroughs online to try and find what I had missed. Maybe this won't happen to you, but I will advise you to be very thorough. You do not want to accidentally run into any spoilers while attempting to progress through the game.

I spent roughly 10 hours playing this game and see potential for another playthrough. I received the game in a Humble Monthly Bundle and would expect this game to go on sale frequently. Add it to your wishlist and you won't regret picking it up on sale.

================Pros==================
Gameplay - This unique and clever gameplay has you picking out data to gather information about suspects.
Graphics - I really enjoyed that graphics, especially the aesthetic of the photos and social media posts.
Story - The story is quite engaging, its really interesting to snoop around peoples internet presence and get to know them 
through their emails and "facebook" posts. It has a lot of twists and turns and some really great choice moments.
Sound design - The sound design here is pretty stellar. Especially the music in the intro, it gave the game a really black mirror vibe, which suited the game tonally.
Interface - The interface was so surreal. Performing computer operations and browsing the internet on a fake system was odd but brilliant.
Techinal - Game ran perfectly.

==============Cons ================
Gameplay - The gameplay can be frustrating at times, you want the outcome to go one way but you aren't able to find the right info. Sometimes I sacrificed the way I wanted the story go just to progress. 

===========Conclusion================
Orwell is defintely worth the buy, especially at such a reasonable price. There are lots of surreal moments that blew me away and a story that's very gripping at times. I wanted to point out that, while I like they added extra stuff to read and extra pages, it makes the world feel more lively but on the other hand it can be quite strenious trying to get the whole story but not wanting to read everything because a lot of it isn't necessary to read.

This was a hell of a game. It’s one of an emerging genre of… ‘interface’ games, I guess. Like Her Story, you are literally your character in the game - what you see on screen is what your character sees, and you interact in the same way. Because of this, the game is incredibly immersive and therefore, at points, really tense!

Let me stop myself before I get too deep in here. In Orwell, you play as, ostensibly, yourself, hired as an ‘investigator’ in this new program called Orwell situated in a different country. In that country, a bomb has just exploded in a plaza, killing two and wounding a dozen or so people. Moments before the bomb went off, a woman was spotted crossing the plaza and getting on a bus. That woman had been arrested months before for assaulting a police officer in that very same plaza during a protest. Could she be connected to the bomb? Your task is to slowly collect information on her, and the people around her. What information you upload to the system cannot be taken back, and you get to choose what the narrative of what happened becomes. You can take an innocuous joke between friends and upload it, taking it out of a friendly context and giving it a sinister cast. You can shift a bias on a person by only uploading the worst of what they said, but not uploading good things about them. In this story, YOU are the faceless watcher, the cog in the wheel, that would be impeding the heroes of a more traditional story.

Holy shit, does it work.

I blasted through the game’s five chapters in one sitting, about four and a half hours on Saturday night. Nobody in this game is 100% good or bad, and there’s a lot of nuance around protesting for the ‘right’ reason in the ‘right’ way that is especially topical for me, right now, as a young woman living in an America I never really thought I’d be living in. This game doesn’t deliver any hard and fast morals at the end, it doesn’t take a definitive stance, and offers three different endings for the player to eventually pick. The game offers up a scenario and leaves it up to you to decide what you think is right… or at least, what you think is the least wrong.

The game isn’t perfect - it wears a little thin when you’re going back and achievement gathering. Like a Telltale game, once you see the constraints of the ‘world’ of the game, the illusion dissipates pretty quickly. There are a lot of real-time sections (text conversations, phone calls) that, while immersive the first time around, made me really wish I had a fast forward button for the fourth or fifth time I sat through the conversation. These are absolutely small gripes, however, and I would strongly urge anyone to pick up this game - especially while it’s still on sale.

Does a passive infrared scanner like they used to use or a cube-type holo-scanner like they use these days, the latest thing, see into me - into us - clearly or darkly? I hope it does, he thought, see clearly, because I can't any longer these days see into myself. I see only murk. Murk outside; murk inside. I hope, for everyone's sake, the scanners do better. A decent game but can't help but feel the game is a little bit TOO much on rails, what with highlighting all the relevant info. Had they given more conflicting info opportunities, or included an option to not highlight all vital info, and instead leaving it up to you to decide, that would have been a great inclusion.

Having said all that, the storyline is quite enjoyable, and sometimes depending on the info you upload and what you think is the truth, could skew your vision on what is right and what is wrong.

Some people have said that one side is hard to side with due to their characters being unlikeable for most of the storyline, but I think this might come down to how you feel about "Big Brother" and affiliated limitations to privacy and control.

As a game, there is not much to it. All clicking and dragging accross to the relevant file, so if you have a rubbish PC, you'll be fine, just leave your keyboard in the cupboard, because aside from entering your name at the beginning, you won't be needing it.

"War is peace.
Freedom is slavery.
Ignorance is strength."

It is one of the most notable quotes from a breathtaking dystopian novel George Orwell's 1984 about totalitarian government. It's also one of my favorite novels of all time and it introduced me to dystopian genre in literature. Some people said 1984 was a self-fulfilling prophecy because government now can keep an eye on their people much easier thanks to technology. They can read your e-mails, chats, watch your moves through cameras, and probably know who you are.

Even if there's cryptography can encrypt our data, I sometimes think that privacy is still a myth.

Only a few minutes in, I'm already hooked to this game. We were 'chosen' to be a controller of Orwell system in order to maintain peace and security in a city. You're given access to read news, websites, someone's e-mails account, private chats, record calls, and even read someone's bank transaction. Unfortunately, there was a bomb explosion that killed citizens and we must find the real culprit based on the data we've got. But, do the data really tell us the truth? Or are we not capable enough to distinguish which one is the truth and which one is a lie?

It's a good game, but don't believe the hype too much. 
It wants you to feel like you choose how what information you want to put forward, but unfortunately, in game, you often feel forced to submit information you don't want to, or guess what information that has to be submitted for you to progress. 
Sometimes it's counter-intuitive too, when the game tells you to not submit false information, then gives you obviously false information, and forces you to submit it. It never lets you be completely free, never lets you fail completely or do it your way. 

But it's still an interesting story, and fun detective work. 
Then comes the ending. For me, it ruined it. It has multiple endings, but for me it was just between choosing doing things you don't want and that wouldn't feel like something you or your character would do. 
That's too bad, since the ending is kind of the lasting impression you bring with you once the game is over. 
Disappointed. At last I had to choose one of them just to finish the game, but at that point it wasn't me playing the game anymore. People are calling it almost a visual novel, and that's kind of what it is. Promises more gameplay than it delivers. 

I'll recommend it, and call it decent. A great idea that could and should have been made better.

Incredible little game. Impressive branching storytelling, inconspicous decisions matter down the line.

Orwell is a must for anyone who still thinks today that they have "nothing to hide". This games gives a great perspective on the benifits and problems with govermental actions to "protect the people". Basic and interesting mechanics with choices that affect outcomes rather significantly, Orwell will make you question what your values are and the usage of such powers to either mend or destroy people's lives.

The soundtrack of the game blends well into the actions and situations occuring. A mix of tense anticipation, dread or even moments of pure solemness are all there for you to experience and delve into. It is something which you don't think about too much but when you look back at how you reacted, you see a fantastically crafted story reinforced by a well suited soundtrack that at worse stirs your emotions.

Orwell however is quite short and sometimes I do encounter moments where I'm not sure how to progress. However, more often than not when a game like this makes you question every decision you make as if people were real, it doesn't feel short at all and it does keep you at the edge of your seat at times.

Elements like breaking the fourth wall, relavence to today's big stories like the NSA leak back then and the serverity of decisions you make are just some of the things that turned Orwell into not just a game, but a story, statement and as mentioned a question of your very own morals.

Fantastic game and looking forward to the next iteration of Orwell.

Take George Orwell's 1984 and distill it into a game where the premise is to spy on the conversations of others in order to find the truth out about a bombing that occurred. It's an interesting concept and one that kept me playing till completion. Different outcomes based on whether you give the correct data, or choose to even send information that you gather. Honeslty it feels more like what we may be seeing in the not to distant future for our own goverment, and definitely opens up a dialog on just how secure we should be, and the moral/ethical boundaries that one is willing to cross for safety.

The game is worth is price - that is, it will entertain you for a few hours. 

The story it tells is thrilling and you feel responsibility for your actions. It's all over in about four hours and replayability value is limited (sure, you could make a few different choices, but the story generally remains the same). 

There are two things I wish for. The game being less of a novel and more of a "strategy game" of discovering different paths via submitting different data, but not such luck, the game is extremely linear. 
And the story making more use of its topic. The irony of activist group debating how government survelience is overstepping the bounds, while player evesdrops on them is actually pretty chilling, but I was hoping for more interesting conclusion then "spying on people is wrong". All the ingredients were there, just the ending left me a little dissapointed.

Minor complaint is, that the super ultra datamining system is not able to locate a phone number of a person you know by name, but that really just something that made me smile rather then annoy me. Still, like I said, I don't feel cheated. It's a short, fun game well worth its modest price.

Every choice you make matters. Many games and VNs advertise this, but may be a little more lax in terms of letting you make some "wrong" choices yet still get the outcome you want. Orwell is not one of those. Depending on what you choose to upload to Orwell will determine the consequences the characters you're tasked with tracking will face. Achievements can also be obtained or compromised from being able to be obtained depending on the actions you take.

The game was longer than I expected, which was great, and the conclusions you can obtain feel very much like a solid way to wrap up the story. Getting into the whole plot took a little time as it felt kind of slow in the beginning as you learn the basics of what to do and how to do it as well as feeling more interested in the story and characters themselves. However, it picks up quickly and while the very beginning may feel a little bland, it's still enough to keep you interested and wanting to find out more.

The soundtrack worked well with the game. It was more ambiant background music, which I liked as it wasn't distracting so it didn't take away from the gameplay and more serious atmosphere the story creates. The changes from calm to tension and panic were abrupt as was the change in mood of the game, keeping you alert.

You'll find yourself doing a lot of thinking about what information you want to reveal about someone to Orwell and what you think is okay to leave out, especially at the end of the game as everything draws to a close.

I do wish the live conversations you spy on would go a little faster, particularly the chat ones. I understand that sitting on the screen while the other person has the "..." as their text bubble for a few seconds is to make it feel more realistic, but at times I felt some replies could've been a little quicker.

There's replay value both for collecting all the achievements as it's impossible to get them all in one play through, and both to see how the story changes and what conversations you spy on will pop up, as well as of course seeing how differently the lives of the characters are affected.

I got Orwell while it was on sale for a few dollars less than full price, but I would still say it's worth whatever you invest. There's a lot of reading, so be prepared for that. Orwell makes you reflect on what it means to have privacy, if there should be a limit to that, when it should be breached, and what privacy means as a whole. Especially with how we use and rely on digital devices for communication and many other uses. Orwell was unlike other games I usually play, but I'm glad I picked this up. It's worth a go.
